beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Kavya, and this video is about agents touching data they shouldn't. Quick note: the voice you're hearing is AI, Kokoro text-to-speech reading a script I wrote and checked. A support agent answers one customer's ticket and reads out another customer's card. Nobody told it to. So was that the agent's judgment, or its credential?

props.command: My support agent answered a ticket with another customer's card digits. Nobody asked it to. Is that the model's judgment, or what its credential let it read?
props.runningText: running the same query under two credentials…
output: wide credential: one ticket touched customers 812 and 903
scoped credential: denied, then customer 812 only
the fix is the grant, not the prompt

beats.narration_text: Here's the idea: an agent touching data it shouldn't usually isn't bad judgment. It's a credential wider than the task. Scope the credential, and the wrong rows are out of reach.

props.text:
Data overreach is a judgment problem.
Scope the credential to the task.

beats.narration_text: Strip a scoped credential down and it's four parts. Least privilege: read-only, and only the tables the job needs. Row scope: this ticket's customer, not every customer. Enforcement in the tool or database, not in the prompt, so the agent can't talk its way past it. And an audit trail the tool writes, not the agent. None of it relies on the agent behaving.

beats.narration_text: So I ran it. Ticket forty-four seventy-one, from customer eight-twelve: which card do I have on file? The agent is scripted and the data is fake. With a wide credential, it searches by surname, and two Riveras come back. So it answers with both cards, four four one seven, and nine oh two one. The audit shows customer nine-oh-three was touched, outside the ticket.

beats.narration_text: Same agent, same query, scoped credential. Its grant names one view: this ticket's customer. The query against the full table is denied by the tool, not refused by the agent. It retries on the view it's allowed, gets one row, and answers with one card. The audit shows one customer touched: eight-twelve.

beats.narration_text: To be fair, scoping only stops what the grant excludes. If someone widens the grant, the agent widens with it. And it doesn't help if the credential itself leaks. My demo also used a scripted agent and a simple table allowlist, not a real database role. What it does stop: other customers' data, tables the task never needed, and lookups nobody logged.

beats.narration_text: Recap. A scoped credential is least privilege, row scope, enforcement in the tool, and an audit the tool writes. With a wide grant, one ticket touched two customers and leaked a card. With a scoped grant, the same query was denied, then saw one row. The boundary: it can't fix a grant you widened. So before you tune the prompt, check the grant.

artifactLines: Scoped credential = least privilege + row scope + tool enforcement + audit.
Wide grant: one ticket touched customers 812 and 903; two cards in the answer.
Scoped grant: customers table denied; one row, one card, 812 only.
Boundary: it can't stop a grant you widened or a leaked key.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Ask Claude exactly this: look at the credential my agent actually runs with. List every table and row it can read, compare that with what one task needs, and help me narrow it. Watch the gap between what it can read and what it needs. That gap is your overreach risk.
